claims.text: A qualifying high-entropy alloy is a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
The superconducting transition temperature of qualifying high-entropy alloys is governed predominantly by valence electron count.
Adjusting the relative proportions of constituent elements can tune the alloy's valence electron count.
Changing valence electron count modifies the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level in a homogeneous BCC or similarly structured phase mediates superconducting behavior.
Changes in the density of states near the Fermi energy affect electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength is critical for superconductivity in the proposed alloy.
Increasing valence electron count is expected to enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling from higher valence electron count may increase the superconducting transition temperature.
Lower valence electron count reduces the available electronic states and decreases the superconducting transition temperature.
Transition temperature will vary systematically with valence electron count when the single-phase structure and processing conditions are maintained.
Higher-valence-electron-count samples are expected to show an increase or other distinct change in transition temperature relative to the baseline.
The transition-temperature shift may be on the order of a few kelvin.
Disorder and microstructural defects may compete with the proposed valence-electron-count effect on transition temperature.
The hypothesis is applicable only while the alloy remains a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Composition ranges that cause phase segregation or significant structural change fall outside the hypothesis's boundary.
A lack of systematic or statistically significant correlation between transition temperature and calculated valence electron count would falsify the hypothesis.
